definition.text: The part of biodiversity that matters for farming: the variety of plants, animals and microbes, at gene, species and ecosystem levels, that sustains food and farm production.

facts.text: It is managed by farmers, pastoralists, fishers and forest dwellers and gives rural livelihoods stability, adaptability and resilience.
It supports food, nutrition and livelihood security and is critical for climate adaptation and mitigation.
About 6,000 species are commonly used for food, by a conservative estimate.
75% of the 115 major crop species grown worldwide rely on pollinators.
It is threatened by urbanization, deforestation, monocultures, abandonment of traditional practices and Westernized diets.
Its loss leads to genetic erosion, including the loss of locally adapted landraces and breeds.
Agrobiodiversity provides income through food and raw materials and by supporting services such as pollination, pest control and nutrient cycling.

definition.text: The decline in the number of crop species grown and in the genetic variety within each crop.

facts.text: Over the past 50 years both genetic diversity within crops and the number of species commonly grown have fallen sharply.
It threatens food security because people depend on ever fewer varieties of ever fewer crops.
The Irish potato blight of 1846, which contributed to one million deaths, struck because only two vulnerable potato varieties were planted.
When rice grassy stunt virus spread in the 1970s, only one of 6,273 varieties tested was resistant.

definition.text: Conserving species or genetic material away from their natural habitat, in places such as seed banks, genebanks, botanical gardens and cryobanks.

facts.text: It is considered a fairly reliable way to keep genetic diversity over the long term because stored material changes little.
Over 7 million samples are held in 1,750 genebanks worldwide.
In situ conservation, by contrast, lets species keep evolving in response to natural and human pressures; practitioners recommend combining both.

definition.text: The genetic variety of bird and mammal species, breeds and populations used for food and farming.

facts.text: About 8,800 breeds of birds and mammals within 38 species are used for food and agriculture.
This diversity can be held in live animals or in stored material such as frozen semen or embryos.

definition.text: The average species diversity found within individual sites at a local scale.

facts.text: R. H. Whittaker introduced it together with beta and gamma diversity.
Whittaker's idea was that a landscape's total diversity (gamma) depends on local diversity (alpha) and on how much sites differ (beta).
No consensus exists on the right spatial scale, so it can be measured for subunits of any size.
Researchers often measure it with species richness, the Shannon index or the Simpson index.

title: Effective number of species
article: Diversity index#Effective number of species or Hill numbers

definition.text: The number of equally common species that would give the same average species abundance as the real, uneven community.

facts.text: It has been proposed as a universal measure of species diversity because it is easier to grasp than diversity indices.
Its values for different orders q are called Hill numbers; the order sets how much weight rare versus abundant species get.
At q = 0 it equals species richness; larger q gives more weight to the most abundant species and a smaller diversity value.
Most common diversity indices are simple transformations of it.

definition.text: The normal rate at which species go extinct through Earth's history, outside mass extinction events.

facts.text: Extinction is a normal part of evolution, and the background rate measures how often it happens naturally.
It is the yardstick for showing how much faster species are vanishing today.
It is roughly one extinction per million species-years; at that rate one bird species would go extinct about every 400 years.
Under normal rates species typically last 5–10 million years; mammal species average about 1 million years.
Background rates have fallen over the Phanerozoic, which has been linked to increasing ocean oxygenation.

title: Beta diversity

definition.text: A measure of how much species composition differs between sites, defined as the ratio of regional to local species diversity.

facts.text: Whittaker introduced it alongside alpha and gamma diversity.
Whittaker's form says how many completely distinct subunits there would be if total and average diversity stayed the same but no species were shared.
Many types now exist, including absolute, Whittaker's and proportional species turnover.
Studies disagree on patterns: in Borneo, moths showed higher beta diversity in primary forest but trees showed it in logged forest.
Invasive species appear to raise local diversity while lowering beta diversity.

contested_note: Studies reach conflicting conclusions about beta-diversity patterns, likely because they use different spatial scales.

definition.text: Formulas that express beta diversity as the amount by which a whole dataset's diversity exceeds that of an average site.

facts.text: Additive partitioning gives absolute species turnover; dividing it by alpha diversity gives Whittaker's species turnover.
For two sites with presence-absence data, Whittaker's turnover equals one minus the Sørensen similarity index.
Dividing absolute turnover by gamma diversity gives proportional turnover, equal for two sites to one minus the Jaccard index.
